1:
Gill states the objection: if grace abounded where sin abounded, some might say it were best to continue in a sinful course. Robertson hears the opening as a debater's phrase and an echo of the rabbinical method of question and answer, and notes that the verb is a deliberative subjunctive meaning to tarry. Wesley marks the advance: the Apostle had earlier only denied the consequence and here removes its very foundation. Theodoret says the same of the method — the disavowal shows the inconsistency, but he is not content with a bare condemnation and treats the subject another way. Ellicott sets the chapter in the argument's architecture: the Apostle is again drawn into one of those subtle casuistical questions that so attracted him, but returns at once to the root ideas of his own system, having dealt already with justification by faith and passing now to union with Christ, the one juridical and the other not. Calvin makes it an accusation: those who imagine gratuitous righteousness given apart from newness of life shamefully rend Christ asunder.

The denial draws a protest from Clarke, who insists the Greek means let it not be, by no means, far from it, and is not properly rendered by our God forbid, since however well that expresses the sense it is not proper to make the sacred name so familiar. Barnes renders it flatly, it may not be. Calvin observes that some take the words for mere indignant reproof, but the Apostle commonly answers so even while carrying a long argument, rejecting the slander first by an indignant negative and then disproving it carefully.

On the clause that follows the two grammarians converge. Ellicott corrects that are dead to that died, citing a commentator on holding the strict aorist against the perfect, since the Apostle regards the whole change — from sin to righteousness, from bondage to freedom, from death to life — as summed up in one moment. Robertson gives the same parsing and dates it, that we died to sin when we surrendered to Christ. Barnes draws the argument from the fact rather than the tense, that the dead cannot act as if alive.

What baptism is said to do divides the bench across every school it has. Robertson is most guarded: rendering the preposition into makes Paul say that union with Christ was brought to pass by means of baptism, which is not his idea, for Paul was no sacramentarian; baptism is the public proclamation of what has already happened. Clarke keeps it at that level: to be baptized into Christ is to receive the doctrine of Christ crucified and to take baptism for proof of that faith and of the obligation to live by its precepts. Barnes likewise makes it a profession by which sin is renounced. Ellicott goes further, glossing it as incorporation into communion with Christ and into his mystical body; Calvin further still, holding it beyond question that we put on Christ in baptism and are baptized for this very end, that we may be one with him. Cyril is boldest: let no one suppose baptism merely the grace of remission of sins, or even of adoption, as the earlier baptism conferred remission only, since while it purges our sins and ministers the gift of the Spirit it is also the counterpart of the sufferings of Christ. Wesley stands between: in baptism we are through faith ingrafted into Christ and draw new spiritual life from this new root. Theodoret turns it back on the objector: thou hast renounced sin, become dead to it and been buried with Christ, and how is it possible then that thou shouldst admit that same sin? Henry adds the warning the argument invites: unholy professors may have had the outward sign of a death unto sin and yet never have passed from the family of Satan to that of God.
4:
Three take the burial for a plain reference to immersion; one concedes it without conceding the point. Gill says baptism is called a burial with manifest reference to the ancient and only way of administering it, by dipping, a person being covered in water as a corpse with earth; Clarke draws the picture out, the whole body put under so that the man seems drowned and dead, and rising seems to have a resurrection to life; Wesley notes the allusion in a phrase. Barnes grants that this is the idea which would strike the great mass of unprejudiced readers, and that it cannot be proved beyond objection, but insists that the Apostle's main scope lay elsewhere. Ellicott takes the burial structurally: it is the consequence of death and the seal set upon it, showing no revival possible, and the one step that separates death from resurrection. Calvin puts the transition as a knot: the Apostle passes from a fellowship in death to a fellowship in life, and the two are joined indissolubly. Theodoret says the sacrament itself teaches us to fly from sin, carrying in it the representation of the Lord's death. Chrysostom stands back to describe the epistle: the Apostle here continually digresses into exhortation instead of dividing the letter as he does elsewhere, doctrine first and moral instruction after, blending the second with the subject throughout so as to gain it an easy admission.

What it means to be planted together is the entry's real division, and Barnes stands alone. He takes the word, which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, to mean sown at the same time, the figure being of grain sown together and springing up together. Everyone else makes it growth into rather than growth beside. Clarke reports that our translation does not express the sense, the plants meant growing the one upon and in the other and drawing sap from it, as the mistletoe on the oak or the scion on its stock; Ellicott says the metaphor is of parasitic growth applied to natural growth, the idea being a bud or graft reckoned as part of the stock it is set in; Robertson derives the adjective from the verb to grow together. Calvin presses hardest: grafting designates not a conformity of example but a secret union by which we are joined to Christ, so that reviving us by his Spirit he transfers his own virtue to us, the graft having life or death in common with its tree. Theodoret finds the resurrection already in the change of word, since whatever is planted springs up again; and Cyril reads the verse against those who would make the sufferings apparent only, since what Christ endured for our salvation he suffered in reality and not in appearance.

Why the old man is called old gets three different answers and what he is gets a fourth. Gill takes it for the corruption of nature, called a man because it dwells in us and rules and has its several members, and called old because it is the poison of the old serpent. Wesley makes it coeval with our being and as old as the fall. Calvin refers the epithet not to age but to relation, the old man being so called as the Old Testament is with reference to the New, since he begins to be old only when a commencing regeneration destroys him by degrees; and he identifies him with the whole nature we bring from the womb. Theodoret denies exactly that: it is not our nature but our evil inclination that is here called the old man. Ellicott takes a middle course, the old self being that congeries of evil habits acquired in heathenism, killed ideally if not actually in our baptism — where Robertson objects again that this took place not at baptism but was only pictured there, having happened when we died to sin.
7:
How much is contained in freed is the question, and the answers spread across the bench. Ellicott and Robertson agree that the word is the one elsewhere rendered justified: Ellicott glosses it absolved, the dead man being no longer liable to have sin charged against him, and Robertson parses it as a perfect, so that the man stands justified. Ellicott then sets the verse out as formal reasoning — the general proposition, the major premise, adduced to prove the particular one that he who is ethically dead is no longer sin's slave. Calvin grounds the argument on what death does rather than on what the word means: if death destroys all the actions of life, we who died to sin ought to cease from the actions sin exercised while it lived; and he takes the word for reclaimed from bondage, as a man is freed from a charge when a judge absolves him. Clarke starts from the same rendering and travels much further, asking whether it does not mean that the man who has received Christ by faith and been made partaker of the Spirit has had his old man and all his evil propensities destroyed, so that he is not merely justified from sin but delivered from it. Wesley divides it neatly in two, freed from the guilt of past and from the power of present sin, as dead men are from the commands of their former masters.

Two argue from outside the vocabulary altogether. Barnes takes the sentence for a proverb and reports a rabbinic saying to match, that when one is dead he is free from commands, a man who dies being exempt from his master's dominion. Theodoret needs no proverb and simply asks who ever yet saw a dead man invading another's marriage-bed, or imbruing his hands in bloodshed, or committing any other item in the catalogue of iniquities. Gill spends his space fencing off the wrong death: a natural death is not meant, since that is the effect of sin and inflicted as punishment for it, and is so far from being an atonement, as some have fancied, that many who die in their sins will rise in them.

On the clause that Christ dies no more they divide four ways. Barnes reads it as sufficiency: he will have occasion to make no other atonement, the one made being enough for all, so that he is beyond the dominion of death. Robertson turns the same fact into a controversy, quoting the maxim that Christ's particular death occurs but once and calling the verse a complete refutation of the sacrificial character of the mass. Ellicott makes it the security of the believer: the eternal subsistence of the life of Christ guarantees the permanence of our own, and were it possible for that life to fail, the whole fabric which faith builds upon it would fall to the ground. Calvin heads off the implication the words seem to carry, that death once ruled over Christ. Giving himself up to death for us he did in a manner surrender to its power, but so that it was impossible he should be held bound by its pangs or swallowed up in them, submitting to its dominion only as it were for a moment. Gill supports the fact rather than the inference: the resurrection is well attested, foretold by the prophets and by Christ himself, affirmed by angels, witnessed by the apostles and by the Spirit.

Clarke draws the exhortation: if we are risen indeed with Christ we should seek the things above, since sin has no more dominion over the man who walks in humble obedience to an indwelling Christ. Theodoret adds the posture the argument requires, that having been buried with Christ we should be dead indeed unto sin and await the resurrection.
10:
Two of them, from opposite ends of the bench, warn against pressing the parallel. Clarke quotes a Latin commentator who renders the clause that Christ died on account of sin, taking the dative for the expiation of sins, and who adds that men die to sin in one way and Christ in another, the Apostle being fond of parallelism, in interpreting which much caution is needed. Calvin says the same in his own idiom, that we must still observe what is suitable to Christ in this form of speech, and supplies at the next verse what he calls the definition of that analogy. Barnes takes the clause of design, that the death was meant to destroy sin and make atonement for it; Wesley compresses that into four words, to atone for and abolish it; Robertson fixes the adverb as meaning once and once only, not once upon a time. Ellicott makes it the last sacrifice Christ made to sin, freeing him from its dominion for ever. Theodoret draws a consequence nobody else draws: since Christ died once and could not die again, possessing now an immortal body, we too enjoy one baptism and are not to expect a second.

The exhortation to reckon is the hinge of the chapter. Ellicott calls it the theoretical application to the readers, who are to regard themselves as insensible and inaccessible to sin but living in close allegiance to God. Barnes makes the deadness as complete as that of the dead in their graves toward this world. Clarke sets the halves against their pattern — die as truly unto sin as he died for sin, live as truly unto God as he lives with God. Calvin marks that the Apostle does not stop at the mortifying but adds the living, since we die while living whenever we renounce sin. Robertson takes the imperative for complete proof that the Apostle does not mean baptism makes a man dead to sin and alive to God, that being a spiritual operation only pictured there; the verse is a plea to live up to the ideal of the baptized life. Theodoret puts it as a demand on the body, to display it dead to the inworking of sin while embracing the life after Christ. Henry enters one qualification: unholy lusts not being quite rooted out in this life, it must be the Christian's care to resist their motions.

What kind of rule sin exercises is the last question, and Theodoret corrects the figure the others use. Clarke calls the clause a personification, sin being a king or ruler or tyrant who holds the desires of the mind and the members of the body under his control and governs the body by working on the passions. Theodoret separates the two words Clarke runs together: a tyranny is exercised over those who submit unwillingly, a reign over consenting subjects — so we are exhorted no longer to agree to sin's government, its reign having been overthrown by the incarnation. Calvin concedes the residue and denies it the throne: though sin dwells in us it is not to be so vigorous as to reign, the power of sanctification being superior to it. Gill guards the exhortation from an inference: it supposes no natural power of free will, being addressed to persons who had the Spirit. On the epithet mortal the grammarians differ only in emphasis: Ellicott sets it at variance with the immortal life just described, Robertson glosses it as subject to death, adding that self-indulgence is inconsistent with trust in a vicarious atonement, and Barnes thinks it chosen to recall the tendency of the flesh. Cyril alone comes at the verse from the Lord's Prayer: a pure soul can say with boldness thy kingdom come, and he who has heard that sin must not reign, and has cleansed himself in deed and thought and word, will say it.
13:
The governing figure is military, and how far to press it divides them. Ellicott insists on the strict sense: the word is not instruments but arms or weapons which sin is to wield, and he carries the metaphor to the end of the chapter, where the wages of sin is the soldier's pay. Theodoret ties it back to sin's government: having spoken of a reign, he mentions in strict keeping with it the artillery of that reign, and teaches the way of victory, since the weapons sin uses against us are our own members. Robertson lets the word out again as an old term for tools of any kind, and presses the tense of the prohibition instead, which forbids a habit rather than an act.

What the members are is disputed between two of them. Barnes takes them for the members of the body — hands, feet, tongue — a specification of what the previous verse covered by the general word body. Gill takes them for the powers and faculties of the soul, citing a version that renders the word simply your souls. Clarke leaves the anatomy alone and draws a rule of conscience nobody else states: it is no sin to be tempted, the sin lying in the yielding — while it exists only in the solicitation it is the devil's sin, and by yielding we make it our own.

On the promise that sin shall not have dominion, four voices from four schools converge on one formula. Clarke describes the law as that which exacts obedience without giving power to obey, and condemns every transgression without providing for its removal. Wesley calls it a dispensation of terror and bondage which shows sin without enabling us to conquer it, and grace the merciful dispensation that brings complete victory. Theodoret says nature no longer fights singly but has the grace of the Spirit for her assistant, the law before grace having taught what was to be done and afforded no help. Calvin, dismissing without ceremony the expositions that have little appearance of truth, gives as most probable that the letter of the law is meant, which cannot renovate the soul, against the grace of the Spirit. The others qualify the promise rather than explain it. Gill grants that sin remains after conversion and has great power to hinder good and effect evil, seeming as though it would regain its dominion; Robertson says only that it shall not lord it over us, even if not yet wholly dead; Barnes reads the words as at once a statement that sin ought not to rule and a conviction that it will not; Clarke adds that if a man becomes subject to it again that is the effect of his own choice or negligence.

The objection is then raised a second time, and Robertson alone shows that it is not the same objection. The verb here is an aorist, asking whether we may commit occasional acts of sin, where the verb at the opening was a present and asked whether we may continue in a life of it. Ellicott notices a change of dress rather than substance: the Apostle returns to a difficulty very like the first but answers it under a different metaphor, no longer death to the one and life to the other but freedom from the one and service to the other. Calvin explains why the objection had to be anticipated: the wisdom of the flesh is ever clamorous against the mysteries of God, men supposing that when the law is removed as the rule of life all discipline falls to the ground. Theodoret reports the method: the objection is noted because of the gainsayers, first reprobated by pointing out its absurdity, and only then answered at length. Barnes adds the form it would take: those pardoned by grace might feel themselves released from any obligation to be holy.
16:
Ellicott finds a whole doctrine in the apparent redundancy. It looks like a tautology, he says, but teaches a deep ethical truth — what you make yourselves, that you become, the habit you form ending as your second nature. Calvin insists the preceding denial was no bare expression of abhorrence, since a confutation follows at once from the contrary supposition, the yoke of Christ and that of sin being so contrary that no one can bear both. Theodoret says it is not possible to obey two lords at once; Clarke puts the alternative plainly, that sin is the service of Satan and righteousness the service of Christ; Henry states the rule flatly, that every man is the servant of the master to whose commands he yields himself. Robertson takes the figure for his answer to the question just raised: men are slaves of the one they obey whatever their profession, and slavery is the argument against occasional sinning.

The thanksgiving that follows embarrasses everyone, and they repair it the same way. Gill says the Apostle cannot be thanking God that these men had been servants of sin, than which nothing is more disagreeable to him, but that they are now free of that drudgery. Barnes draws the argument from their own experience, a ground of gratitude to him. Robertson finds the fault in the English, since there is no whereas in the Greek and the verb is an imperfect: the Apostle is not grateful that they were once slaves of sin but that, having been so, they turned from it. Clarke re-points the whole sentence, so that it reads, thanks be to God that although ye were the servants of sin, nevertheless ye have obeyed from the heart. Calvin explains why the thanksgiving stands there: it teaches that the change came not by their own merit but by the special mercy of God.

What they were delivered into divides the bench along confessional lines. Wesley, Clarke and Henry all read the word as a mould. Wesley presses it hardest — literally it is the mould into which ye have been delivered, an allusion carrying an instructive admonition, that our minds being pliant and ductile should be conformed to the gospel precepts as liquid metal takes the figure of its mould. Clarke calls it the mould of teaching into which they were cast; Henry says they were delivered into the gospel as into a mould. Ellicott will have none of the metal: it is a pattern of teaching, an express moral rule of life, to whose direction they were handed over.

On the freedom itself Gill is the most restrictive voice in the chapter. It is not freedom from a sinful nature, nor from a corrupt heart, nor from vain thoughts, nor from sinful words, nor from sinful actions altogether, but from the damning power of sin, the sentence having been executed on Christ instead. Clarke reads the verb as the technical term for the manumission of a slave, and finds a second personification here, sin and righteousness both being made persons. Robertson denies that anything lies between: we have simply changed masters, set free from that tyrant only to be enslaved to righteousness, with no no-man's-land in this warfare. Ellicott answers the paradox with a liturgical phrase, that this is a service which is perfect freedom. Calvin argues from the unreasonableness of the thing, that a man made free ought to maintain his freedom; Theodoret says it in a line, that having cast away the slavery of sin and taken the yoke of righteousness a man cannot bear the latter and obey the former. Wesley alone stands back and sets out the Apostle's whole method to this point in a numbered table, from bondage to sin, through the knowledge of sin by the law, to the revelation of the righteousness of God and the faith that embraces it.
19:
What the Apostle apologises for gets five answers. Chrysostom alone refers it not to the manner of speech but to the severity of the demand: having required great strictness of life, charging us to be dead to the world and to incline no way toward sin, he seemed to be saying something too much for human nature, and speaks so to show he makes no exorbitant demand. Robertson makes the apology narrower still — the Apostle begs pardon for having used the word slaving of righteousness, though he thinks it a good word for a time when self-assertiveness and personal liberty bulk so large. Clarke takes the phrase for a known idiom of the Greek writers meaning what was easy to be comprehended, as distinct from the high flights of the poets and the studied obscurity of the philosophers. Calvin distinguishes substance from manner: the accommodation is only in the manner, as when the Lord announced earthly things while speaking of heavenly mysteries, suiting himself to an ignorant people.

What the infirmity is divides them along a different line. Ellicott makes it intellectual, the dulness of their understanding, so that the mystical phrase used just before might have been beyond them where this figure is clear even to a preoccupied mind. Barnes makes it moral, the word meaning weakness as opposed to vigour, and the flesh often denoting the corrupt passions. Theodoret is on the same side: he suits his exhortation to their nature, being aware of the passions that contend in a mortal body.

On being free from righteousness Barnes makes the phrase carry more weight than anyone else — they were not at all under its influence, which is a strong expression of total depravity and proves they had no native goodness. Robertson keeps it light: they wore no collar of righteousness but did as they pleased. Calvin repeats the contrariety, that sin and righteousness are so opposed that a man who devotes himself to one necessarily departs from the other, the two being set apart so that we may see each more clearly. Clarke denies any third possibility: if we cannot serve God and Mammon we cannot serve Christ and Satan, so we must be either sinners or saints — and he quotes a verse he thinks well meant and mistaken, in which a man professes himself equally bent to good and evil and so both a devil and a saint. Wesley turns it into a claim, that they ought now to be as zealous in serving God as they once were in serving the devil. Theodoret puts the asymmetry from the other end: they fulfilled the precepts of sin only and did not receive the laws of righteousness at all.

The question about fruit is answered chiefly by refusing it the name. Henry says the pleasure and profit of sin do not deserve the name of fruit, since sinners are but ploughing iniquity, sowing vanity and reaping the same; shame came into the world with sin and is still its certain effect. Gill asks what it profits a man to amass the riches of the Indies if his soul is lost by it. Robertson has them holding ashes in their hands. Theodoret makes the silence itself the answer — it is idle to ask the gains of sin, since they confess its injury by saying nothing; and however barefaced a man may be, he cannot but feel shame once the enjoyment is over. Calvin admires the method: he could not more strikingly have expressed his meaning than by appealing to their conscience and confessing the shame as it were in their own person. Ellicott alone attends to the pointing, reporting that some place the question earlier — what fruit had ye at that time? things of which ye are now ashamed, for their end is death — though he judges the received construction best.
22:
Theodoret counts the antithesis in threes: God is opposed to sin, holiness to shame, life everlasting to everlasting death. Calvin makes the parallel from the other side: as a twofold end of sin was mentioned before, so now a twofold end of righteousness — sin brings in this life the torments of an accusing conscience and in the next eternal death, while we now gather holiness and hope hereafter for eternal life. Clarke turns it into a chiasm: as being free from righteousness is the finished character of a sinner, so being made free from sin is the finished character of a genuine Christian. Ellicott states the change plainly, that they are no longer without fruit; Barnes marks the correspondence with the earlier verse, that they are now delivered from sin's dominion as they were once free of righteousness. Robertson finds the asymmetry in the grammar: eternal life stands in the accusative as object of the verb, where the death set against it stood in the nominative.

The word for wages then draws four different derivations. Barnes takes it back furthest, to what is bought to be eaten with bread and thence to the pay of the Roman soldier, since it was once the custom to pay soldiers in such things, so that the word means what a man earns or deserves. Robertson keeps to the military sense and adds the sting, that sin pays its wages in full and takes no cut. Calvin reports the reading that makes the comparison disparaging, an allowance of meat such as the Greeks sometimes meant by it, a wretched reward doled out to sinners; but he thinks the Apostle rather condemns indirectly the blind appetites of those whom sin ruinously allures. Theodoret alone reads the word as the last term of a single figure running through the chapter: sin having been said to reign, then to tyrannize, and its weapons having been called our own badly disposed members, the reward it pays is consistently called a soldier's wages, as the Apostle names military pay elsewhere.

What death is owed divides them by scope. Gill takes it of every sin, original and actual, lesser and greater, and the death owed as a corporeal one, coming neither from the original constitution of men nor merely from divine appointment but from sin and the decree of God on account of it. Clarke means the second death and everlasting perdition, and turns the earning into a reproach — every sinner earns it by long, sore and painful service, and what pains men take to get to hell, toiling at sin early and late, so that divine justice would be in their debt if it did not pay them their due. Wesley refuses to choose and takes all three: temporal, spiritual, eternal.

The broken antithesis at the end is the one thing the whole bench agrees on, across the line that usually divides them. Ellicott states it: the natural opposite of wages would be wages again, but that is inappropriate here, so the Apostle substitutes the free gift — for in spite of all their sanctification they will still not have earned eternal life. Wesley calls the difference remarkable, that evil works merit their reward and good works do not, the former demanding wages where the latter accept a gift. Clarke puts it as a maxim: a man may merit hell but cannot merit heaven. Robertson says it in five words, that eternal life is God's gift and not wages, both the death and the life being alike eternal. Cyril takes the closing phrase for a text of its own, observing that many are the proofs concerning the life eternal, and that when we desire to gain it the Scriptures suggest the ways, declaring at one time that it is by faith — though he sets out only a few passages and leaves the rest to the diligent.
